new_statements.quote: Stress: Stress is not a primary phoneme, although we may recognize different degrees of stress. It is something related to the intonation, and may perhaps be considered as a feature of intonation. There is not a consistent record on stress in my material, and for the time being we shall not be concerned about it.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-opened the mirror copy (16 pp., 6.76 MB, scan, no text). Rendered pp. 1-16 in one slotted page render call (150 dpi) and read scan pages 1, 4, 11, 12 as images; then ran ONE slotted tesseract (eng) over the 16 renders (no other scanned running) and saved the page-marked scanned as in the mirror; renders deleted. Title page (scan p.1 = printed p.551): 'THE JUI DIALECT OF POAI: PHONOLOGY / FANG-KUEI LI 李方桂', first sentence 'The Jui dialect spoken in Poai 剝隘 in the district of Funing 富寧, Yunnan, belongs to the Northern group of Tai dialects..' -> same work as the citation (BIHP 28: 551-566; printed page numbers visible). The quoted 'Stress:' paragraph is on printed p.562 (scan p.12) exactly…
new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (guib1244 has no catalog record and no stress statement held by the project; all four sources read earlier were silent). First statement for the language: tonal, stress non-phonemic and treated as intonational, no word-stress rule stated.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Po-ai Jui (Bo'ai, Funing) is a six-tone language (six tone phonemes on sonorant-final syllables, three on checked syllables); Li states that stress is NOT a primary phoneme: degrees of stress exist but stress is 'related to the intonation' and 'may perhaps be considered as a feature of intonation'; no word-stress placement rule is given and he explicitly sets stress aside. Supporting remarks: syllable juncture is marked phonetically by 'the onset of stress' (p. 554); vowel-initial syllables 'are usually less stressed' and never utterance-initial (p. 555); utterance-final particles are toneless and carry intonational pitch (p. 561).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-initial syllables (e.g. e: 'one' in mi: hon e: 'once upon a time') 'never occur after a pause or begin an utterance, and are usually less stressed'; when uttered initially or 'in a stressed position' a glottal stop appears (p. 555). Toneless particles at utterance end carry intonation pitch (p. 561). 'There is not a consistent record on stress in my material' (p. 562).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1957 describes the Jui (Dioi/Buyi-type Northern Tai) dialect of Po-ai 剝隘 (Bo'ai), Funing 富寧 County, Yunnan, from one speaker recorded in 1930 -- the variety Glottolog files under Guibian (Yei) Zhuang guib1244 and that the bibliography's Nong 2020 / Luo 2024 papers revisit. Johnson's two SIL reports concern the Central Taic Nong, Dai and Min Zhuang of Wenshan Prefecture, with Yei Zhuang only as a neighbouring Northern Taic group.

tone_statements.quote: 西林土黄村壮语有 8 个调类，6 个调值，6 个舒声韵，4 个塞声韵(见表 5)。 … 声调说明： 1) 西林土黄村壮语的声调调类与壮语标准音的调类一致，都有八个调类； 2) 壮语标准音中，第 1 调与土黄村壮语第 2 调调的值相同，均为 24 调；第 2 调分别与土黄村壮语第 5 调的调值相同，均为 31 调；第 3 调与土黄村壮语第 6/7/8 调调的值相同，均为 55 调；后两个调类都有长短音形式； 3) 土黄村壮语中的第 3 调与第 4 调的调值相同，第 6 与第 7 调的短元音形式调值相同，且第 3 调与第 8 调的长、短元音形式调值相同，均为 55 调。
tone_statements.translation: Xilin Tuhuang-village Zhuang has 8 tone categories, 6 tone values, 6 smooth(-syllable) tones and 4 checked(-syllable) tones (see Table 5). ... Notes on the tones: 1) the tone categories of Tuhuang Zhuang coincide with those of standard Zhuang, both having eight categories; 2) standard Zhuang tone 1 has the same value as Tuhuang tone 2 (24); standard tone 2 the same as Tuhuang tone 5 (31); standard tone 3 the same as Tuhuang tones 6/7/8 (55); the latter two categories have long- and short-vowel forms; 3) in Tuhuang Zhuang tones 3 and 4 have the same value, the short-vowel forms of tones 6 and 7 have the same value, and tone 3 [sic] and the long/short forms of tone 8 have the same value, 55.

tone_statements.quote: 7.1. Northern Zhuang tonal development. Northern Zhuang tone systems are generally very close to the paradigmatic 5X2 profile that results from splitting according to the Voiced-Low Principle (Brown 1975) having the top three boxes in each column in the high tone category and bottom box in the low tone category. … Type 3 In this system voiced-low splitting occurs—with the exception of syllables possessing original preglottalized initials in tone C, which were assigned to the low tone category, a situation found at points (9), (39), and (40). This division corresponds to the Bouyei system of Guizhou Province and also the system Gedney found for Yay.

tone_statements.quote: p. 562: "Stress: Stress is not a primary phoneme, although we may recognize different degrees of stress. It is something related to the intonation, and may perhaps be considered as a feature of intonation. There is not a consistent record on stress in my material, and for the time being we shall not be concerned about it." -- p. 561: "Tones: A syllable has usually a tone, although there are some syllables which are toneless. These are the particles which occur often at the end of an utterance or before a pause. They usually carry the pitch of the intonation that must be symbolized in a diffenent way from the tones. [...] There are six tone phonemes, indicated by tone-letters placed after the syllable. 1) Rising, from mid-low to mid-high 2) High level 3) Mid-high level 4) Mid-level 5) Mid-low level, or simply low 6) Falling, from middle to low"

sources.quote: 7.1. Northern Zhuang tonal development. Northern Zhuang tone systems are generally very close to the paradigmatic 5X2 profile that results from splitting according to the Voiced-Low Principle (Brown 1975) having the top three boxes in each column in the high tone category and bottom box in the low tone category. … Type 3 In this system voiced-low splitting occurs—with the exception of syllables possessing original preglottalized initials in tone C, which were assigned to the low tone category, a situation found at points (9), (39), and (40). This division corresponds to the Bouyei system of Guizhou Province and also the system Gedney found for Yay.

sources.note: Sec. 7 treats Zhuang tone splitting from Proto-Tai *A B C D by initial class; sec. 7.1: Northern Zhuang systems are close to the paradigmatic 5x2 voiced-low split (Type 1); Type 3 = voiced-low split except that original preglottalized initials in tone C go to the LOW category, found at points 9 (Hechi), 39 (Tianlin) and 40 (Guangnan N), matching Bouyei and Gedney's Yay; Baise-area points split tone C similarly with some DL splitting. Tone values per site for the remaining Guibian points (36-38) fall on pp. 167 ff., not scanned (20-page scanned cap).
